How Systems Find Similarity in Millions of Data Points in Milliseconds: HNSW and IVF
Whether in searches, recommendations, or AI-based systems, there’s a fundamental problem being solved all the time: quickly finding similar items in a gigantic universe of data.
It was while studying the book Designing Data-Intensive Applications that I delved deeper into two of the main strategies that make this possible in vector databases: HNSW and IVF.
In this article, I’ll explain intuitively how these algorithms work and why they’re so important.
The Problem: Search in High Dimensions
When working with embeddings, each item (text, image, product, etc.) is represented as a vector in a high-dimensional space.
The simplest way to find similarity would be to compare the query vector with all other vectors.
The problem is that this doesn’t scale well at all.
•
1 million vectors → 1 million comparisons
•
100 million → 100 million comparisons
For real-time applications, this simply isn’t viable.
This is where Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) algorithms come in.
HNSW: Navigating Like on a Map
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) solves this problem elegantly.
Instead of comparing everything with everything, it organizes the data as a multi-layered graph.
Intuition
Imagine exploring an unfamiliar city:
•
First, you take highways to get close to the right area
•
Then, you use smaller streets to find the exact destination
HNSW works exactly like that.
How It Works
•
Each vector is a node connected to other similar vectors
•
There are multiple layers in the graph
•
Upper layers: few connections, long jumps
•
Lower layers: more connections, refined search
Search Process
1.
Starts at the highest layer
2.
Quickly navigates to promising regions
3.
Descends layer by layer, refining the search
4.
Finds the nearest neighbors
Advantages
•
High accuracy
•
Excellent performance for online queries
Disadvantages
•
High memory usage
•
More complex index construction
IVF: Reducing the Search Space
IVF (Inverted File Index) follows a different approach.
Instead of navigating a graph, it divides the vector space into groups (clusters).
Intuition
Imagine looking for a book in a library:
You don’t check every book. First, you go to the right section.
IVF applies exactly this idea.
How It Works
1.
Vectors are grouped into clusters (usually with k-means)
2.
Each cluster has a center (centroid)
3.
During search:
•
The query vector is compared with the centroids
•
Only the closest clusters are selected
•
Search happens only within those clusters
Advantages
•
Very memory efficient
•
Scales well for large volumes
Disadvantages
•
Can lose accuracy depending on the number of clusters
•
Sensitive to clustering quality
HNSW vs IVF: When to Use Each
Both approaches solve the same problem, but with different strategies.
HNSW
•
Best for scenarios requiring high accuracy
•
Ideal for online queries
•
Uses more memory
IVF
•
Best for very large datasets
•
More memory efficient
•
May sacrifice a bit of accuracy
In practice, many systems combine techniques (like IVF + quantization or hybrid HNSW) to balance cost and performance.
Why This Matters
These algorithms are the foundation of many modern applications:
•
Semantic search
•
Recommendation systems
•
RAG with LLMs
•
Similarity search in images
Without these optimizations, working with embeddings at scale would be impractical.
Conclusion
What seems simple to the user—finding something relevant in seconds—relies on deep decisions about data structures and algorithms.
HNSW and IVF are two clear examples of how thoughtful engineering makes modern systems viable.
And the more we work with AI and large-scale data, the more understanding these mechanisms shifts from a differentiator to a necessity.
